solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mone's expensive purchase from Spooner back in the day?

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so his version of a phrase has its initial sounds exchanged

parts.note: a costly boat; Michelle Mone, a British businesswoman and Conservative peer, was widely reported in connection with a luxury yacht

explanation.surface: A wry dig at a peer's pricey boat, set alongside the old clergyman who mixed up his words.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of 'the dear yacht' and you get THE YEAR DOT. Mone is Michelle Mone, a British entrepreneur and member of the House of Lords whose finances made headlines.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a British idiom for a very long time ago, the remote past, matching the nostalgic expression.

clue.text: Husband running EU rail transport business

parts.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband

indicators.note: something running is in motion and not settled, so the letters move about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A husband operating a European rail freight company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' reads as operating the business, but it tells you to rearrange the letters after the H.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a haulier is a road or rail firm that carries goods commercially for customers.

clue.text: The old way to introduce a fungus

indicators.note: introducing something means putting it inside, so one piece is slotted into the others

parts.note: ye is an archaic spelling of the
taken as written
ST, street, is a common abbreviation for a way

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned method for bringing a fungus into a culture or dough.
explanation.walkthrough: Ye is the archaic spelling of 'the', as on mock-olde shop signs; 'way' is the usual crossword street abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast is a single-celled organism belonging to the kingdom of fungi, used in baking and brewing.

clue.text: Frisky, 50, in a married relationship

indicators.note: frisky means lively and playful, so the letters jump about out of their usual order

parts.note: the number written out as a word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lively fifty-year-old still playful within a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The number must be spelt out as a word before its letters join 'in a' to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Affinity has a formal legal sense of kinship created by marriage, as opposed to blood relationship.

clue.text: Oh… a lad v giant did become quite a story!

indicators.note: to become is to turn into something else, so the letters change into a new form

parts.words: Oh… a lad v giant did
parts.note: all fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone marvelling at how a boy against a giant turned into a legendary tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface already describes the biblical fight, which makes the clue almost an &lit: every letter of 'Oh a lad v giant did' is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical tale of the shepherd boy felling the Philistine champion is one of the most famous stories ever told.

clue.text: The black stuff beginning to tempt real ale fans to the north

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading north means going upwards, so these letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: CAMRA, the Campaign for Real Ale, is a British organisation of traditional beer enthusiasts

explanation.surface: Guinness, the black stuff, luring real ale lovers to the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The black stuff' is a nickname for Guinness, which suits the beer surface, but here it means road surfacing. CAMRA is the Campaign for Real Ale, a British beer group.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac is the dark asphalt surface used on roads, jokingly called black stuff for its colour.

clue.text: Bank regularly swindled

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: A bank that has been routinely cheating its customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' suggests the money sense, but the definition is the slope at the edge of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A riverbank is the edge or flank of the water, and side is a synonym for that sloping edge.

clue.text: SS boss, wartime captive sporting black eye

indicators.note: sporting something means wearing it on show, so one piece carries another within it

parts.note: a shiner is slang for a bruised eye
POW stands for prisoner of war

explanation.surface: A Nazi SS commander and a prisoner of war with a bruised eye.
explanation.walkthrough: SS looks like the Nazi paramilitary, but it is the prefix for a steamship, so its boss owns the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: SS marks a steamship's name, and the person in charge of such a vessel commercially is its owner.

clue.text: Iced over before the German crunch match?

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: taken as written
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: A pitch frozen solid ahead of a vital game against Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iced over' reads as frozen, but 'over' turns the first word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A crunch match settles the outcome of a contest, which is exactly what a decider or final game does.

clue.text: Instrument neighbour returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: to abut is to neighbour, lying next to something

explanation.surface: A neighbour handing back a borrowed musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neighbour' looks like a noun, the person next door, but it is the verb meaning to lie next to.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is a large brass instrument with a deep pitch, a standard example of the category.

clue.text: Part of Hornby set that generates enormous excitement?

definitions.text: Part of Hornby set that generates enormous excitement?

parts.note: surface reading: a piece from a Hornby model railway set, the British toy train brand
setter's reading: a work by the novelist Nick Hornby, his football memoir, whose title names a state of frenzied excitement

explanation.surface: A toy train component that thrills its owner beyond measure.
explanation.walkthrough: Hornby is a famous British maker of model trains, so 'set' suggests a train set; the setter means Nick Hornby, whose memoir of supporting Arsenal is set around a football ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Hornby's 1992 football memoir carries this title, and the phrase itself describes a peak of frenzied collective excitement.

clue.text: Component in engine pump is to need clamping

indicators.note: to clamp is to grip and hold in place, so the run of words holds the answer within it

parts.note: letters running across the last letter of the first word, the next two words and the start of the fourth

explanation.surface: A mechanic saying a pump part needs to be held tight in a clamp.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans four words, starting at the last letter of 'pump'.
explanation.definitionFit: A piston is the sliding cylinder part that moves up and down inside a combustion motor.

clue.text: Ice suit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: underworld slang for precious gems
second meaning: one of the four sets in a pack of playing cards

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice suit' sounds like skating clothes; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice is criminal slang for cut gemstones, and the red lozenge cards form one of four suits in a standard deck.

clue.text: Book trendy seaside resort

parts.note: B is a standard abbreviation for book
right-on means fashionably progressive

explanation.surface: An instruction to reserve a stay at a fashionable coastal town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like the verb to reserve, but it is just the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Brighton is a well-known holiday town on England's south coast, famous for its pier and lively atmosphere.

clue.text: Famous American Good Old Republican boy I have upset

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
O is the abbreviation for old
R stands for Republican

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so in a down entry these letters are turned upside down

parts.note: a lad is a boy
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: A well-known American conservative upset by a young man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good Old Republican' looks like the GOP nickname for the party, but it supplies three single letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gore Vidal was a celebrated twentieth-century US novelist, essayist and political commentator, hence a famous person from the United States.

clue.text: Police informer drug cop reported

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we want a word that sounds like another

parts.note: narc is American slang for a narcotics officer

explanation.surface: An informer tipping off the drugs squad.
explanation.walkthrough: A narc is US slang for a drugs agent; the British slang word for an informer sounds identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Nark is British slang for someone who passes information to the police, a grass or stool pigeon.

clue.text: In the morning, knackered, attacked by surprise

parts.note: a.m. denotes the morning
both are informal words for exhausted

explanation.surface: Someone worn out at dawn and then jumped on unexpectedly.
explanation.walkthrough: Knackered is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: To ambush is to lie in wait and launch a sudden assault, so the past form fits an unexpected strike.

clue.text: Finished port after saying goodbye to daughter

indicators.note: once you bid farewell to something it leaves, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: Dover is the English Channel ferry port
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A port visit ending once a daughter has been waved off.
explanation.walkthrough: Dover is the Kent port facing France; drop its D.
explanation.definitionFit: Something over has come to an end, so the word is a synonym for completed or done.

clue.text: Very independent spoiled child, zero musical skill

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for very
I is the abbreviation for independent
a brat is a spoilt child
O looks like a zero

explanation.surface: A very self-willed, pampered youngster with no musical talent at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a scathing description of a child, but every word but the last two is a building piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Vibrato is the singer's or string player's technique of rapidly wavering pitch, a learned performing ability.

clue.text: Dodge Russian fighter from the east, first-rate

indicators.note: in an across entry, coming from the east means reading right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a MiG is a Russian fighter jet
crack means expert or first-class, as in crack troops

explanation.surface: Evading an excellent Russian pilot coming in from the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodge' looks like a verb, to evade, but it is a noun: a clever trick or contrivance. 'Fighter' suggests a person but is a jet.
explanation.definitionFit: A gimcrack is a showy trinket or ingenious gadget, which older dictionaries also list as a trivial contrivance or trick.

clue.text: Century since Euler discovered hooded garment

indicators.note: to dis-cover is to strip the covering away, so the outer letters are removed

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for century
both mean in the past, as in long ago
the mathematician's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: A garment found a hundred years after the mathematician's time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' looks like found, but it means stripping the first and last letters from the name. A cagoule is a light hooded waterproof.
explanation.definitionFit: A cagoule is a lightweight waterproof jacket with a hood, so it is a hooded item of clothing.

clue.text: Holy See initially having lots of land

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter
acred means owning many acres

explanation.surface: The Vatican, which from its beginnings has owned a great deal of property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holy See' reads as one phrase naming the papacy, but 'Holy' is the definition and only 'See' supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacred and holy are synonyms, both describing what is consecrated or connected with God.

clue.text: First and foremost a lovable rogue

indicators.note: a rogue thing behaves erratically and strays from its order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Describing someone as, before anything else, a charming scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lovable rogue' is a stock phrase, which hides that 'rogue' is the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms meaning most importantly, used to stress the chief point of a statement.

clue.text: Upper-class actor Nicolas showcasing new release

indicators.note: showcasing something means displaying it in a case, so one piece is held inside others

parts.note: U is the standard label for upper-class
N is the abbreviation for new
Nicolas Cage is a Hollywood star

explanation.surface: A posh film star promoting his latest film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New release' looks like a movie launch, but 'new' is a letter and 'release' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncage an animal is to free it from confinement, so the verb is a synonym for set free.

clue.text: Chaotic OBR arranges to host emergency meeting

indicators.note: to host is to have something within as a guest, so the words contain the answer

parts.note: the last letter of the first word, all of the second, and the first of the third

explanation.surface: The UK budget watchdog in disarray, setting up a crisis session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaotic' and 'arranges' both look like anagram signals, but nothing is rearranged. The OBR is Britain's Office for Budget Responsibility, and COBRA is the UK government's crisis committee.
explanation.definitionFit: COBRA, named after Cabinet Office Briefing Room A, is the British government committee convened to handle national crises.

clue.text: British tree and Dutch tree rot

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
the alder is a tree
D is the abbreviation for Dutch
the ash is a tree

explanation.surface: Native and Dutch trees both suffering from decay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rot' looks like the disease affecting the trees, but it is the noun meaning nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Rot is informal British for nonsense or rubbish talk, and balderdash is a synonym for senseless claptrap.

clue.text: Rejected European Union; pound down

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters are turned round

parts.note: the usual abbreviation
lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight

explanation.surface: A Brexit-style rejection of Europe followed by sterling falling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound down' suggests a currency slump; 'down' is the definition and the reversal covers both chunks together.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down and feeling blue are both informal ways of saying sad or low in spirits.

clue.text: Bird starts to fly over winter landscape

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A bird taking off over a snowy wintry scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to fly' reads as a bird taking off, but 'starts' asks for initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fowl is a general word for birds, especially domestic or game birds such as chickens and ducks.

clue.text: Daddy there, desperately in need of a drink

indicators.note: acting desperately means acting wildly and without order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Father over there, gasping for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads naturally as a thirsty dad, so 'desperately' feels like part of the picture rather than a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being short of bodily water leaves a person thirsty and requiring fluids, which is what the phrase describes.
